claim: Simulation-pretrained neural feedforward compensation combined with variable-impedance feedback improves force tracking over tested constant-impedance and velocity-adaptive baselines across several unknown-terrain tasks, subject to a simplified contact model, Lipschitz bounds, observable regression state, and narrow HRI evidence.
epistemic_status: Primary analytical, simulation-to-real, robot-task, and limited HRI evidence; broad safety and universal transfer remain unsupported.
problem_and_setting: Force tracking on unknown terrains across static machining, quasistatic peeling, and dynamic physical-interaction tasks.
method_or_mechanism: A neural feedforward policy is pretrained by deep reinforcement learning on randomized simulated terrains and combined with variable-impedance feedback. Stability, zero-error, and sim-to-real conditions are derived using a simplified dynamic contact couch model and a Lipschitz-continuity condition. Observable system states must be included in the regression vector to avoid over/underfitting.
content_summary: On flat stiffness switches the controller shows short overshoot; on slopes feedforward removes adaptive hysteresis; curved-terrain mean force-error ratio stays below 5%. Peeling success averages 15.6% constant impedance, 57.8% adaptive, and 73.3% DRL; at 5 N, DRL peel-thickness standard deviations are lower for apple, potato, and cucumber. In handshake, combing, and five swabbing tests, DRL reduces force error 55.4% on average and human-effort metric is no greater than adaptive control. HRI lacks cohort/randomization/adverse-event reporting and excludes constant impedance.
synthesis_role: Direct evidence for learned feedforward plus variable-impedance force control and conditional sim-to-real reasoning across heterogeneous contact regimes.
development_link: Advances reactive impedance adaptation with a learned predictive term, while making model validity, state observability, and transfer coverage explicit obligations.

evidence.finding: A simplified couch model and Lipschitz condition yield sufficient stability, zero-error, and transfer conditions; omitting observable states causes over/underfitting.
DRL handles stiffness switches with short overshoot, removes adaptive hysteresis on slopes, and keeps curved-terrain mean force-error ratio below 5%.
Average success is 15.6% constant, 57.8% adaptive, and 73.3% DRL; at 5 N, DRL peel-thickness SDs are 0.058/0.033/0.033 mm versus adaptive 0.106/0.092/0.177 mm.
Across handshake, combing, and five swabbing tests, DRL reduces force error 55.4% on average versus adaptive and measured human effort is no greater; constant impedance is omitted.

boundary_conditions: Simplified contact couch model and required Lipschitz bounds.
Peeling uses three tests per lateral-side/force condition.
HRI lacks reported cohort, randomization, blinding, and adverse events.
Universal grasping and bipedal use remain future work.
assumptions: Simplified contact dynamics represent tested interactions.
Randomized simulation covers real operating conditions.
Reported human-effort metric reflects participant workload.

reported: Regression vectors without observable states cause overfitting or underfitting.
Constant-impedance HRI was omitted due authors' injury concern.
Flat stiffness switches produce transient overshoot.
inferred: General safety and universal sim-to-real transfer are unsupported.
HRI population validity is weak because participant/protocol details are absent.
Excluding one comparator limits HRI comparative inference.
Theory fails if simplified-model, Lipschitz, observability, or coverage assumptions fail.

verification_status: Controller-verified full-text identity and hash; author results and reader inference are separated.
